title: How do you ensure safe concurrent updates in real-time systems (optimistic/pessimistic locking, CAS/atomic, concurrent structures, MVCC, Redis locks)?
shortTitle: Ensuring Safe Concurrent Updates in Real-Time Systems

s1_definition.profdef: Safe concurrent updates mean guaranteeing correctness when many threads or transactions modify the same data at once, avoiding lost updates and race conditions. The main techniques are pessimistic locking (lock the row so others wait), optimistic locking (detect conflicts at commit via a version check and retry), compare-and-swap atomics and concurrent data structures in memory, database MVCC with appropriate isolation, and distributed locks such as Redis locks when coordination spans multiple services.
s1_definition.analogy: If two tellers try to debit the same National Bank of India account at the same time, both might read the balance as one thousand, both subtract, and one update is lost. Pessimistic locking is like one teller locking the account drawer so the other must wait. Optimistic locking is like both working on photocopies but stamping a version number — whoever saves second notices the version changed and redoes their work. Atomic compare-and-swap is a single indivisible "only update if it is still what I expected" move. Distributed locks are a shared ticket across many branches so only one branch acts at a time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Prevent lost updates by choosing the right concurrency control — pessimistic locks, optimistic version checks with retry, atomic CAS, database MVCC/isolation, or distributed Redis locks — according to contention and scope.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Safe concurrent updates mean guaranteeing correctness when many threads or transactions modify the same data at once, avoiding lost updates and race conditions. The main techniques are pessimistic locking (lock the row so others wait), optimistic locking (detect conflicts at commit via a version check and retry), compare-and-swap atomics and concurrent data structures in memory, database MVCC with appropriate isolation, and distributed locks such as Redis locks when coordination spans multiple services.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** If two tellers try to debit the same National Bank of India account at the same time, both might read the balance as one thousand, both subtract, and one update is lost. Pessimistic locking is like one teller locking the account drawer so the other must wait. Optimistic locking is like both working on photocopies but stamping a version number — whoever saves second notices the version changed and redoes their work. Atomic compare-and-swap is a single indivisible "only update if it is still what I expected" move. Distributed locks are a shared ticket across many branches so only one branch acts at a time.

**One line to remember:** Prevent lost updates by choosing the right concurrency control — pessimistic locks, optimistic version checks with retry, atomic CAS, database MVCC/isolation, or distributed Redis locks — according to contention and scope.

sections.s2_technical:
The core danger is the lost update / read-modify-write race: two actors read the same value, each computes a new value from it, and the second write overwrites the first, silently losing a change. Different tools address this at different layers.

Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely and locks the data up front so others block until the holder commits — in SQL this is `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, which holds a row lock until commit or rollback so a read-check-then-update sequence is protected. It is simple and strongly correct but reduces concurrency and risks deadlocks, so you use it only where correctness truly requires it and keep transactions short. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: you read a row with a version column (or timestamp), and on update you say `UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = :read_version`; if zero rows are affected, someone else changed it first, so you detect the conflict and retry. JPA/Hibernate implement this with `@Version`. It scales better under low contention because it takes no locks while thinking, at the cost of retries when conflicts do occur.

In application memory, atomic operations and compare-and-swap give lock-free safety for single variables: Java's `AtomicInteger`/`AtomicReference` with `compareAndSet` update a value only if it still equals the expected one, and concurrent data structures like `ConcurrentHashMap` and `LongAdder` provide thread-safe access without explicit synchronization. At the database level, MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control, used by PostgreSQL, Oracle, and InnoDB) lets readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers and writers without blocking readers, and the chosen isolation level (`READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ`, `SERIALIZABLE`) determines which anomalies are prevented — `SERIALIZABLE` can abort a transaction on a serialization conflict, which the app must retry. For coordination across multiple service instances or non-transactional resources, a distributed lock such as a Redis lock (`SET key value NX PX ttl`, ideally via the Redlock pattern or a library like Redisson) ensures only one instance performs a critical section, with a TTL so a crashed holder's lock expires.

The senior framing is to pick the mechanism by contention and scope: optimistic locking for low-contention database updates that scale, pessimistic `FOR UPDATE` only where a short critical section must be serialized, atomics and concurrent collections for in-process state, rely on MVCC plus the right isolation level for consistency, and distributed locks only when the critical section spans processes or external resources. Always design updates to be idempotent and retryable, because every optimistic and serializable approach assumes the caller retries on conflict.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's account-balance service is hit concurrently: two simultaneous withdrawals from the same account both read the balance, both subtract, and one update is lost, letting the account be overdrawn. The team needed safe concurrent debits. They evaluated optimistic locking with a version column (scales well, retries on conflict) and, for a tightly contended hot account, pessimistic `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, plus in-memory `AtomicReference` CAS for a cached counter.

Our mini-project demonstrates the lost-update race and then fixes it two ways: an optimistic version-check update that retries on conflict, and an in-memory compare-and-swap, proving both eliminate the lost update under concurrency while a naive read-modify-write does not.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an account starting at one thousand, debited one hundred by ten concurrent threads; the correct final balance is zero.

Step 1 — Under optimistic locking, each thread reads the current balance and version, computes the new balance, and attempts a conditional update that only succeeds if the version is unchanged since it read. If another thread committed first, the version no longer matches, the update affects zero rows, and the thread retries from a fresh read.

Step 2 — Because every successful update bumps the version and every conflicting update retries, no debit is lost. After all ten threads finish, the balance is exactly zero and the version has advanced by ten, one bump per successful debit.

Step 3 — Under compare-and-swap, each thread reads the cached balance, computes the new value, and calls `compareAndSet`, which applies the change only if the value still equals what it read; if not, it loops and tries again with the current value.

Step 4 — The CAS loop guarantees no update is clobbered, so the cached balance also ends at exactly zero despite ten concurrent debits.

Step 5 — Both results confirm the safe mechanisms eliminate the lost-update race that a naive read-modify-write would suffer, where several threads reading one thousand would each write nine hundred and lose most debits.

Final output:

```text
Optimistic: 10 x 100 debited from 1000 -> balance = 0.0 (version 10)
CAS:        10 x 100 debited from 1000 -> balance = 0.0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  LOST UPDATE (unsafe): T1 read 1000 ─┐   T2 read 1000 ─┐
                        write 900  ───┘   write 900  ───┘  → one debit lost

  OPTIMISTIC: read(balance, version) → UPDATE ... WHERE version=read
                 match? yes → apply + version++      no → RETRY from fresh read

  PESSIMISTIC: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (row lock) → others WAIT → update → commit

  CAS: do { prev=get(); next=f(prev); } while(!compareAndSet(prev,next))

  MVCC + isolation (DB) | Redis distributed lock (across services, TTL)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Choosing Concurrency Control ═══

  contention?  scope?                     mechanism
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  low | single DB row ───────────────▶ OPTIMISTIC (@Version) + retry
  high | short critical section ─────▶ PESSIMISTIC (SELECT FOR UPDATE)
  in-process single var ─────────────▶ CAS / Atomic*, ConcurrentHashMap
  DB consistency/snapshots ──────────▶ MVCC + isolation (RC/RR/SERIALIZABLE)
  across service instances/resources ▶ DISTRIBUTED LOCK (Redis NX PX + TTL)

  Golden rule: make updates idempotent & retryable; lock only where needed.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Safe Update Strategies ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Optimistic Offline Lock (version column) | CAS loop               │
  │ Strategy: choose control per contention/scope                     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: service exposes each strategy as a method                     │
  │ O: new strategy (pessimistic) = new method                       │
  │ D: callers pick strategy via interface, not internals            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Mechanisms ──
  PESSIMISTIC : SELECT FOR UPDATE | lock held to commit | correct, less concurrency
  OPTIMISTIC  : version check on UPDATE | 0 rows → retry | scales low-contention
  CAS/ATOMIC  : compareAndSet | lock-free single var | ConcurrentHashMap/LongAdder
  MVCC        : snapshots; readers/writers don't block; isolation level matters
  REDIS LOCK  : SET NX PX ttl / Redlock / Redisson | cross-process | TTL safety

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main() → 10 threads
  2.   → debitOptimistic()  [read ver → conditional update → retry on conflict]
  3.   → debitCas()         [compareAndSet loop]
  4.   balances end at exactly 0 (no lost updates)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Safe concurrent updates mean guaranteeing correctness when many threads or transactions modify the same data at once, and the central danger is the lost update: two actors read the same value, each computes a new value, and the second write silently overwrites the first. I address it with the right mechanism for the contention and scope. Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts are likely and locks the row up front with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, holding the lock until commit so a read-check-then-update sequence is serialized; it is simple and strongly correct but reduces concurrency and risks deadlocks, so I use it only for short critical sections where correctness truly demands it. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare: I read a row with a version column and update with `SET ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = :read_version`, and if zero rows change I know someone else updated first and I retry — JPA's `@Version` implements exactly this, and it scales well under low contention because it takes no locks while thinking.

In application memory I use compare-and-swap atomics like `AtomicReference.compareAndSet`, which updates only if the value still equals what I read, and concurrent structures like `ConcurrentHashMap` and `LongAdder` for lock-free thread safety. At the database level MVCC lets readers and writers avoid blocking each other by reading consistent snapshots, and the isolation level — `READ COMMITTED`, `REPEATABLE READ`, or `SERIALIZABLE` — decides which anomalies are prevented, with `SERIALIZABLE` sometimes aborting a transaction that the application must retry. When the critical section spans multiple service instances or non-transactional resources, I use a distributed lock such as a Redis lock with `SET key val NX PX ttl`, ideally via Redlock or Redisson, including a TTL so a crashed holder's lock expires. At the National Bank of India our balance service suffered lost updates when two withdrawals hit the same account, and we fixed it with optimistic version-checked debits that retry on conflict for the common case and pessimistic `FOR UPDATE` for a few hot accounts. The senior framing I always state is to pick the control by contention and scope and to make every update idempotent and retryable, because all the optimistic and serializable approaches assume the caller retries on conflict. The line I always state is to prevent lost updates by choosing the right concurrency control — pessimistic locks, optimistic version checks with retry, atomic CAS, MVCC with proper isolation, or distributed Redis locks.
